rationale: A wins because it turns the missing proof into the story instead of pretending the proof exists. Its headline "the company isn't yet saying how often they get it right" is a clean enterprise-risk angle rooted in the supplied gaps; B's "The no-code database market just became the AI-agent-on-your-data market" tries to declare a market shift from one company's repositioning. B has usable bones, but it keeps drawing maps before it has roads.
gaps_in_A: "employees are the ones left to catch what they get wrong" asserts an oversight workflow the update does not provide. Make it a question about approval, audit trails, and rollback, not a fact.

"the prevailing belief this cuts against: that enterprise AI agents are now trustworthy enough to act autonomously on production data" is a little too broad for the supplied facts. The safer claim is that Airtable is asking buyers to trust agents without public reliability data.

"All four angles are blocked on the same gaps — reliability data, a valuation timeline, and a named customer or on-record exec quote" overgeneralizes. The valuation angle needs valuation history and investor color; the category angle needs positioning copy or an exec; the reliability angle needs error-rate and guardrail data.
gaps_in_B: "The no-code database market just became the AI-agent-on-your-data market" is a billboard-sized overclaim. The update supports Airtable changing its pitch, not an entire market changing.

"Airtable just entered the AI agent market — that changes who it competes with" is plausible but under-built. Without named competitors, buyer comparisons, or analyst framing, it is a hypothesis wearing a headline.
"all-in product pivot" overstates the facts. The update says Airtable is repositioning and launching agents; it does not prove the whole company has made an all-in pivot.
It buries the sharpest enterprise-IT angle as a question: "Is Airtable willing to share any reliability or error-rate data on the agents?" That should have been a full angle, not cleanup copy.
